## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes field methods for estimating Leaf Area Index (LAI),
the total one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground surface area
(m^2^ leaf / m^2^ ground). LAI is a key structural parameter
governing light interception, transpiration, and primary productivity
[@jonckheere2004]. It is used in the EA Program for characterizing
canopy structure at photovoltaic panel sites, restoration areas, and
agricultural plots.

Both ceptometer and hemispherical photography methods estimate an
"effective" LAI that assumes a random spatial distribution of foliage
elements within the canopy. In most real canopies, foliage is clumped
rather than random, and the effective LAI underestimates the true LAI
by 20--50% depending on species and canopy architecture [@chen1997;
@breda2003]. When reporting LAI values, specify whether a clumping
correction has been applied and which correction method was used.
Ground-based LAI measurements also serve as critical reference data
for validating satellite-derived LAI products [@garrigues2008;
@zheng2009].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Indirect optical measurement of LAI using
  hemispherical photography and/or a ceptometer (AccuPAR or equivalent
  linear PAR sensor) at all EA Program field sites
- **Does not apply to:** Direct destructive leaf area measurement
  (harvest methods); satellite-derived LAI products (though ground
  measurements may be used to validate them); root area measurements
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Definitions

- **Leaf Area Index (LAI):** The total one-sided area of leaf tissue
  per unit ground area. Dimensionless (m^2^ m^-2^). Typical values
  range from 0 (bare ground) to 1--3 (grasslands and crops) to 5--10
  (closed-canopy forests) [@jonckheere2004].
- **Effective LAI ($L_e$):** The LAI value obtained from optical
  methods that assume random foliage distribution. Effective LAI
  underestimates true LAI in clumped canopies because light passes
  through gaps between clumps more easily than a random model predicts
  [@chen1997].
- **True LAI:** The actual one-sided leaf area per unit ground area,
  obtained either by destructive harvest or by applying a clumping
  correction ($\Omega$) to the effective LAI:
  $\text{LAI}_{\text{true}} = L_e / \Omega$, where $\Omega < 1$ for
  clumped canopies [@chen1997].
- **Clumping index ($\Omega$):** A dimensionless parameter (0 to 1)
  describing the degree to which foliage deviates from a random
  distribution. Values near 1 indicate nearly random distribution;
  values of 0.5--0.7 are typical for conifer canopies.
- **PAR:** Photosynthetically Active Radiation (400--700 nm).
- **Ceptometer:** A linear array of PAR sensors used to measure light
  transmission through a canopy. LAI is estimated from the ratio of
  below-canopy to above-canopy PAR using the Beer-Lambert extinction
  model [@norman1989].
- **Gap fraction:** The proportion of the sky hemisphere visible
  through the canopy at a given zenith angle. Gap fraction is the
  primary measurement from hemispherical photography and is inverted
  to estimate LAI.
- **Extinction coefficient ($K$):** A parameter in the Beer-Lambert
  model relating LAI to light transmission; depends on solar zenith
  angle and leaf angle distribution.
- **Hemispherical photography:** A technique using a fisheye lens
  pointed upward to photograph the canopy. Gap fraction analysis of
  the image yields LAI estimates [@frazer2001].


## 4. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve measurement design, review data     |
| Trained Personnel | Collect field measurements per this SOP     |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use    |


## 5. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Uneven terrain, tripping hazards from dense vegetation
- **Biological:** Tick and insect exposure in dense canopy understories
- **Heat:** Measurements are often taken in open or partially shaded
  areas during peak growing season
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toe shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Long pants and long sleeves (tick protection in dense vegetation)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).

## 7. Estimated Time

| Task                                 | Time                          |
|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------|
| Site setup and orientation           | 10--15 minutes                |
| Ceptometer measurements (10 points)  | 20--30 minutes                |
| Hemispherical photographs (10 points)| 30--45 minutes                |
| Data download and QC                 | 15 minutes                    |


## 8. Procedure

### 8.1 Measurement Timing

LAI measurements should be taken under uniform overcast skies or
within one hour of solar noon under clear skies [@weiss2004]. Avoid
measurement during patchy cloud conditions, as rapidly changing light
causes inconsistent above-canopy reference readings. For hemispherical
photography, early morning, late afternoon, or overcast conditions
produce the best contrast between sky and foliage [@breda2003].

### 8.2 Sampling Design

1. Determine measurement locations using the project sampling design
   (random, stratified random, or collocated with vegetation transects
   from [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd))
2. At each location, take a minimum of 5 below-canopy readings
   (ceptometer) or photographs (hemispherical) to capture spatial
   variability [@weiss2004]
3. Record GPS coordinates at each measurement location

### 8.3 Method A: Ceptometer (AccuPAR)

1. Power on the ceptometer and set the date, time, and site ID
2. Enter the leaf angle distribution parameter ($\chi$). Use 1.0 for
   a spherical distribution (default for most broadleaf canopies)
   unless species-specific values are available [@norman1989].
3. Take an above-canopy PAR reading by holding the sensor bar
   horizontally in full sunlight (or use the external above-canopy
   sensor if available)
4. Move to the first below-canopy measurement point. Hold the
   ceptometer horizontally at approximately 1 m height (or just above
   the understory layer), perpendicular to the dominant row or canopy
   orientation.
5. Record the below-canopy PAR reading
6. Rotate the ceptometer 90 degrees and take a second reading at the
   same point to account for canopy anisotropy
7. Average the two readings for that point
8. Repeat at each of the remaining measurement points (minimum 5 per
   location)
9. Take another above-canopy reading at the end of the measurement
   sequence to verify that light conditions have not changed
   substantially (within 10% of the initial reading)
10. The instrument calculates LAI internally using the Beer-Lambert
    model:

$$
\text{LAI} = \frac{-\ln(\tau)}{K}
$$

where $\tau$ is the ratio of below-canopy to above-canopy PAR and $K$
is the extinction coefficient (a function of solar zenith angle and
leaf angle distribution). This value is the effective LAI ($L_e$)
and does not include a clumping correction.

### 8.4 Method B: Hemispherical Photography

1. Mount the camera with fisheye lens adapter on the tripod at 1 m
   height (or just above the understory)
2. Level the camera using the tripod's bubble level
3. Orient the top of the image toward magnetic north using a compass
4. Set the camera to manual exposure: use the sky brightness (not the
   canopy) to set exposure. Bracket exposures if uncertain (one stop
   above and below). Exposure settings strongly influence the
   sky/foliage classification threshold and can introduce systematic
   bias in LAI estimates [@breda2003].
5. Take the photograph pointing directly upward (zenith)
6. Record the image number, GPS coordinates, and any notes (e.g.,
   understory density, canopy species) on the field data sheet
7. Repeat at each measurement point

#### Image Analysis

8. Transfer images to the lab computer
9. Analyze using Gap Light Analyzer (GLA) or the `hemiphot` R package
   [@ter-steege2018]:
   a. Threshold the image to classify pixels as sky (gap) or foliage
   b. Calculate gap fraction at multiple zenith angle rings
   c. Invert gap fractions to estimate LAI using a canopy model (e.g.,
      Miller's formula or the ellipsoidal leaf angle model)
10. Report the mean LAI and standard error for each site. Specify
    whether the reported value is effective LAI or clumping-corrected
    true LAI.

::: {.callout-note}
### Ceptometer vs. Hemispherical Photography
The two methods measure slightly different quantities and may not
agree at the same site. Ceptometers integrate PAR transmission along
a linear transect and are sensitive to solar angle and sky conditions;
hemispherical photographs sample the full sky hemisphere and are
analyzed offline, allowing more flexible post-processing. Agreement
between methods is typically within 0.5--1.0 LAI units, but
systematic offsets can occur, especially in heterogeneous canopies
[@thimonier1996; @jonckheere2004]. Using both methods at a subset of
sites allows cross-validation and helps quantify method-specific bias.
:::


## 9. Quality Control

- Take at least 5 below-canopy readings per measurement location to
  quantify within-site variability
- Report the coefficient of variation (CV) across readings; if CV
  exceeds 30%, increase the number of readings
- For ceptometer measurements, verify that above-canopy PAR did not
  change by more than 10% between the start and end of the measurement
  sequence
- For hemispherical photography, visually inspect thresholded images
  to ensure correct sky/foliage classification; manually adjust the
  threshold if needed
- Cross-validate: where possible, compare ceptometer and hemispherical
  photography estimates at the same points [@breda2003]
- When LAI data will be used to validate remote sensing products,
  document the spatial footprint (measurement spacing and extent) and
  the timing relative to the satellite overpass [@garrigues2008]


## 10. Data Management

1. Download ceptometer data to the lab computer within 48 hours
2. Organize hemispherical images by site and date:
   `LAI_SiteID_YYYYMMDD/`
3. Archive raw data and images on the lab shared drive
4. Version-control analysis scripts per
   [SOP-L801](../lab_sops/SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd)

## 12. Training Record

Before measuring LAI independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
2. Demonstrate correct ceptometer operation (power on, set parameters,
   above/below readings, data download)
3. Demonstrate correct hemispherical photography technique (leveling,
   orientation, exposure settings)
4. Process one set of images through gap fraction analysis under
   supervision
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
